A Screen-Reader-Friendly Guide to the Freakonomics Radio Podcast

Jamal Mazrui

September 2026

Abstract

A screen-reader-friendly directory of the podcast Freakonomics Radio, covering 939 public episodes from 2010 to 2026. Each episode links to its audio and lists its metadata in separate, alphabetically sorted fields.

Freakonomics Radio Directory

Freakonomics Radio, hosted by Stephen Dubner, explores the hidden side of everything, using the tools of economics to tell surprising, rigorously sourced stories about how the world really works. Episodes cite their sources and interview the researchers behind them.

This directory covers 939 public episodes, 2010 to 2026. Each episode’s title link plays its audio; an Episode page link follows the title when the show offers a separate page; and the metadata on record appears one kind per field, in alphabetical order: Date, Duration, Episode, Season, and Summary, each shown only when available. Titles ignore a leading “A”, “An”, or “The”; people are sorted by surname; all sorting ignores case.

Episodes are grouped by year, earliest first, and within each group they are in date order, oldest first, so a show reads the way it unfolded. Appendixes reorder them by date (newest first), by title.

For current details, the linked pages are authoritative. This directory was compiled by Jamal Mazrui from the show’s public feed.

Introducing Stephen J. Dubner’s new podcast, “Tell Me Something I Don’t Know”

Date: November 15, 2016

Duration: 00:53:22

Summary: “Tell Me Something I Don’t Know” is a live game show hosted by Stephen J. Dubner of “Freakonomics Radio.” He has always had a mission: to tell you the things you thought you knew but didn’t, and things you never thought you wanted to know, but do. Now, with “TMSIDK,” he has a new way of doing just that. This new show is still journalism, still factual – but disguised in the most entertaining, unexpected, and occasionally ridiculous conversation you’re likely to hear. Audience contestants come on stage and try to wow a panel of experts with a fascinating fact, a historical wrinkle, a new line of research – anything, really, as long as it’s interesting, useful and true (or at least true-ish). The panel – an ever-changing mix of comedians, brainiacs, and other high achievers – poke and prod the contestants, and ultimately choose a winner. And there’s a real-time, human fact-checker on hand to filter out the bull. This debut episode features Barnard College president Debora Spar, New York Public Library president Tony Marx, and comedian Andy Zaltzman; Jody Avirgan from FiveThirtyEight handles the fact-checking. You can subscribe now on iTunes. And don’t worry, Freakonomics Radio isn’t going anywhere – this is just a special bonus episode of Dubner’s new side gig

Andrea Bayer , deputy director for collections and administration at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Lonnie G. Bunch III , Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution. Victor Ehikhamenor , Nigerian writer and artist. Patty Gerstenblith , professor emeritus of law at DePaul University College of Law. Tom Wilkening , professor of economics at the University of Melbourne. RESOURCES: ” After Seizures, the Met Sets a Plan to Scour Collections for Looted Art ,” by Robin Pogrebin and Graham Bowley ( The New York Times, 2023). ” Nigeria Benin Bronzes: Buhari Declaration ‘Blindsides’ Museum Officials ,” by Barnaby Phillips ( B.B.C., 2023). ” Shared Stewardship and Ethical Returns Policy ,” by the Smithsonian Ethical Returns Working Group (2022). ” Protecting Antiquities: A Role for Long-Term Leases? ” by Michael Kremer and Tom Wilkening ( Working Paper, 2015). 686. Why Is It So Hard to Find an NFL Quarterback?

Date: September 11, 2026

Duration: 00:58:20

Episode: 686

Summary: For decades, teams have tried (and mostly failed) to predict which college quarterbacks will thrive in the pros. Is the science finally catching up? Stephen Dubner speaks with a scout, a psychologist, a data warrior, and a Hall of Fame quarterback who nobody wanted. SOURCES: Scott Goldman , sports psychologist, owner of the Athletic Intelligence Quotient. Dan Hatman , director of scouting development at the Scouting Academy. Stephen Smith , founder and C.E.O. of Kitman Labs. Kurt Warner , Hall-of-Fame quarterback, N.F.L. Network analyst. RESOURCES: ” Head in the game: the impact of cognitive abilities on performance of National Football League quarterbacks ,” by R. Thomas Boone, Nicholas Zambrotta, Andrew Manocchio, and James Bowman (Frontiers in Psychology, 2025). ” The Quarterback Prediction Problem: Forecasting the Performance of College Quarterbacks Selected in the NFL Draft ,” by Julian Wolfson, Vittorio Addona, Robert Schmicker (Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports, 2011). EXTRAS: ” The Merger You Never Knew You Wanted ,” by Freakonomics Radio (2025). ” The Rooney Rule ,” series by Freakonomics Radio (2024)

How to Be a Double Unicorn, with John Urschel | Better in Person

687. Are Prediction Markets the Best Forecasting Tool Ever — or Just Another Casino?

Date: September 18, 2026

Duration: 00:48:39

Episode: 687

Summary: The promise is that they can beat the experts at predicting inflation, elections, and FDA approvals. But right now, roughly 90 percent of the action is sports. Is this a future we want to bet on? Stephen Dubner speaks with, among others, the C.E.O. of Kalshi. (Part one of a two-part series .) SOURCES: Robin Hanson , professor of economics at George Mason University. Nicole Kagan , head of research at Kalshi. Tarek Mansour , co-founder and C.E.O. of Kalshi. RESOURCE: ” Kalshi and the Rise of Macro Markets ,” by Anthony Diercks, Jared Dean Katz, and Jonathan Wright (Federal Reserve Board, 2026). ” Slowly, Then All At Once: What Mamdani’s Victory Tells Us About Information Aggregation ,” ( Kalshi Research , 2026). ” Futarchy: Vote Values, But Bet Beliefs ,” by Robin Hanson (2000). ” The Use of Knowledge in Society ,” by Friedrich Hayek (American Economic Review, 1945). EXTRAS: ” The Economics of Sports Gambling ,” by Freakonomics Radio (2019). ” How to Be Less Terrible at Predicting the Future ,” by Freakonomics Radio (2016). ” The Folly of Prediction ,” by Freakonomics Radio (2011)

688. When Is a Bet Not a Bet?

Date: September 25, 2026

Duration: 00:50:32

Episode: 688

Summary: That’s the question at the heart of a battle between Kalshi and state gambling regulators. As prediction markets boom, there are other questions, too — about insider trading, market manipulation, and whether the public has turned against them. (Part two of a two-part series .) SOURCES: Gary Gensler , former chair of the S.E.C. and the C.F.T.C. Robin Hanson , professor of economics at George Mason University. Nicole Kagan , head of research at Kalshi. Tarek Mansour , co-founder and C.E.O. of Kalshi. RESOURCES: ” Shall We Vote on Values, But Bet on Beliefs? ” by Robin Hanson (Journal of Political Philosophy, 2013). EXTRAS: ” Are Prediction Markets the Best Forecasting Tool Ever — or Just Another Casino? ” by Freakonomics Radio (2026). ” He Helped Clean Up the Last Crash. Does He See Another One Coming? ” by Freakonomics Radio (2026). ” The Economics of Sports Gambling ,” by Freakonomics Radio (2019)
